reason: The attack I expected to land was printing drift, because this poem has two printings that genuinely differ. I pulled the Academy of American Poets full text, which credits the December 1922 Crisis and states the poem is in the public domain, and set it beside the text as The Weary Blues (Knopf, 1926) prints it. They are NOT identical: the poets.org text gives "Bare;" where The Weary Blues gives "Bare.", "a'climbin'" where the book gives "a-climbin'", "Don't you sit down on the steps;" where the book gives "Don't you set down on the steps", and semicolons where the book has full stops. So drift is real in this poem, and a citation that names the wrong printing would be a false citation. It does not touch the three lines being shipped. Both printings close identically: "For I'se still goin', honey, / I'se still climbin', / And life for me ain't been no crystal stair." Every apostrophe, the comma after "honey", the comma after "climbin'", the full stop at the end. The shipped wording therefore exists in the named printing AND survives into the book, which is the strongest position a line can be in. LOCATOR: correct on both counts. They are the last three lines, and they do follow "Don't you fall now", which is the line immediately before them in both printings. SPEAKER: the poem is a mother's speech to her son throughout, from "Well, son, I'll tell you" onward, so "(the mother)" is right, and this is one of the two speaker traps the brief carries generally: a character's line goes in the source in parentheses, and it does. ATTRIBUTION: not on the misattribution list, not contested anywhere I could find, and the December 1922 Crisis date is given independently by poets.org, the encyclopaedia article and the Wikipedia article. GATES: shipped.js returns shipped [], near [], Hughes at 1 for the year (month 5), cap 3, not banned, and he appears once in the month's 54 candidates, so rule 8 is clean. SCOPE: 1922, a poem, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory; the dialect is the poet's own and needs no warning; this is the month's theme stated outright. SOURCE LINE: 95 characters, leads with the name, no dash, curly apostrophes only, no straight double quote. TAG Poetry is the form. ONE REMARK the editor may want: since the shipped three lines are the same in both printings, the citation is safe as written, but if the editor ever wants belt and braces, adding the 1926 Weary Blues after the Crisis date would still fit the 140 characters.
